articles.title: Hopkins Sports in Review (Nov. 9 - 15): Hockey and soccer keep on rolling!
articles.description: The season is coming to a close, and as such we've officially reached the NCAA playoffs! Hopkins has had some strong performances across the last few years, and the hope is that we can win some championships in a push for this year's Learfield Directors' Cup. With that being said, let's take a look back at some of the best performances from the Blue Jays from this past week. Field Hockey: W (2 - 0), W (1 - 0), W (2 - 1 2OT) In what has been an incredibly successful season for the Women's Field Hockey team, the Blue Jays travelled to the NCAA tournament fresh off a Centennial Conference Championship. Their first matchup was against unranked Denison University at Homewood Field. Hopkins registered the first score of the match in the first period thanks to a penalty shot from sophomore midfielder Sarah Chilton. Their second score came in the third quarter from sophomore midfielder Catherine D'Arcy, cementing a dominant win for the home side. Next up were seventh-ranked Stevenson University in a match that took place in Medford, Massachusetts. It was never going to be an easy contest for the Blue Jays, but a gritty display of defense in the first quarter helped them stay competitive. Junior goalie Jessica Lapidus was responsible for four saves that enabled Hopkins to keep it a level scoreline heading into the second period. Smelling blood, the Blue Jays managed to score with four minutes left in the first half in what ended up being the deciding moment of the game. The tuff-est matchup of the week came in their quarterfinal game against Tufts University, the top ranked team in the nation. Hopkins got off to a great start, with sophomore forward Evie Hamm scoring the opening goal of the contest in the first quarter. Tufts managed a response in the second period, tying the game up at one a piece. Some brilliant goalkeeping from Lapidus allowed Hopkins to survive regulation without conceding another goal, at which point it was anyone's game. The first period of overtime saw Tufts take eight shots to Hopkins' three, but none of them managed to find the back of the net. It was a 73rd minute shot from senior forward Sophia Albano that broke the tie and hand Hopkins a victory in a major upset. The team will travel to Geneva, NY this Friday to take on third ranked Christopher Newport in the NCAA semifinal! Football: W (17 - 3) With this being the final game of a disappointing regular season, the odds were not in favor of Hopkins coming out on top of a strong Franklin & Marshall team. Nevertheless, the game is won on the field, not on paper, and Hopkins hoped to put up a tough performance against their conference rivals. The Diplomats received the ball first, but the drive ended quickly with a punt back to the Blue Jays, a good start! Unfortunately, Hopkins could not make much out of their opening possessions either as the ball flipped between the teams. Franklin & Marshall kicked a field goal at the end of the first quarter, but there was not a substantial difference separating the two teams. However, once the second quarter came around, the Blue Jays were able to establish some rhythm on offense, leading a five minute 70-yard drive that resulted in a touchdown. They ended the quarter with a field goal, pushing the margin to seven at the half. A couple of empty possessions to begin the half were quickly forgotten after a quick two-minute drive capped off by a 28-yard receiving touchdown to sophomore wide receiver Alex Orecchio made it a two-score game. The Blue Jays defense remained stout, not allowing any kind of positive field position to the Diplomats as they held them to zero points through the final three quarters. Franklin & Marshall only registered 57 yards of total offense in that stretch of time, including a game ending interception to seal the victory! While the season may not have been a complete success, this was a resounding finish for a team that showed resilience, winning their final four games of the year. Women's Soccer: W (4 - 0), W (1 - 0) Ranked eleventh in the nation, the Hopkins women's soccer team entered the NCAA tournament with high hopes of post-season success. First on their schedule was unranked Rivier College in a game played at home. It didn't take Hopkins too long to get on the scoreboard as freshman forward Katie Derby put one away in the 20th minute of the contest. Rivier only managed to make one shot all day, meanwhile the Blue Jays were able to score three more goals from their 22 shots, a completely dominant display. Next up was Hamilton University on Sunday afternoon in a must-win game for the Blue Jays. While it was not the same one-sided affair as against Rivier, Hopkins came out strong, scoring a first half goal thanks to senior forward Caroline Marcus netting one in the 24th minute. Hamilton was able to stay within an arm's length of the Blue Jays, but a sensational performance from sophomore goalkeeper Ella Kruntchev saw her save five shots from the opposition. Hopkins were outshot six to zero in the second half, but the defense stayed resolute and allowed them to edge out a narrow one goal victory over the Continentals. The Blue Jays will face conference rivals Swarthmore this Saturday in the Sweet 16 of the NCAA tournament!

articles.title: Now that you don't have to be perfect: Netflix's East of Eden chooses to be good
articles.description: Having first heard about Netflix's recent adaptation of John Steinbeck's classic novel East of Eden through an event Hopkins hosted at the Bloomberg Center in DC, I had no idea what a gem was waiting for me. Adapted by Zoe Kazan, the seven-episode miniseries follows two generations of brothers in the Trask family in the United States at the turn of the twentieth century, amid the settling of California and rapid social and economic transformation. Although, I want to stress that this is an adaptation that doesn't require you to know anything about these characters. As I will mention, it does a great job of letting them present themselves to the viewer: through their actions, through what they say but mostly through what they try, and often fail, to hide. The show starts with Florence Pugh, who is also an executive producer of the series and plays our female protagonist, Cathy Ames, narrating: "I believe there are monsters in this world born from human parents." Then, Cathy drags herself through literal mud to barely reach the doorstep of the Trask brothers' farmhouse. Covered in blood and clearly beaten almost to death, she is welcomed, almost by instinct, by Adam Trask (Christopher Abbott). Meanwhile, his brother Charles (Mike Faist) remains skeptical. After all, how could an honest woman have ended up in such a degrading situation without anyone in town knowing her? To some, this might be, to keep with the biblical allegory, an Eve-bites-the-apple moment. In a sense, it is, because it is the catalyst for the continuation of the show, given that Cathy will later marry Adam and give birth to the next generation of the Trask family. But did it mean an evil change of tide? You will have to find out by giving the show a shot. Although, maybe from the title of this review, you can imagine that this is the central question, not the answer, that drives the storytelling of Zoe Kazan's East of Eden: can things be inherently good or evil? Cathy Ames, our antihero, encapsulates that beautifully by offering the viewer a plethora of nuance. It is in Florence Pugh's commendable acting (I have yet to see a transition from crying to laughing so terrifying and gripping as hers) and in the very core writing of her character. Cathy does horrible things, including, but not limited to: murdering, stealing and manipulating. And the show doesn't try to brush it off. These actions are given a carefully calculated space to exist: they don't suffocate the plot into a Machiavellian coloring of Cathy's character, nor are they the setup for a villain-origin story where we find out that "everything was for a greater, more ethical cause." She is just human. And a (very) flawed one, of course. I also quite liked how refreshing it was to see a woman in a historical drama who was given the means and empathy by her writers to show all of herself - beyond just her oppression within the misogynistic setting she lives in. Another highlight of the show was the dynamics of brotherhood. As we meet Adam and Charles in the first part of the series, and then Aron and Cal in the second, we basically meet iterations of the Cain and Abel biblical myth twice. For those unfamiliar with it, it is the first murder in the Bible, which tells the story of Adam and Eve's sons and how brotherly jealousy drove Cain to kill his own brother. That is portrayed with different subtexts in each of the Trasks' generations, and I promise the setup of these sibling dynamics is worth your attention, especially because of the color the "Cain" figures, Charles and Cal, bring to the overall East of Eden narrative. Every. Single. One. of these brothers has qualities and flaws, which I wasn't expecting given the heavy biblical subtext, in a way that makes you constantly rethink your curiosity about these characters. And in the middle of all this, we are introduced to Lee (Hoon Lee), the caregiver of Aron and Cal when they are left orphaned by their mom and dad (the latter being more of a symbolic abandonment). Similarly to the other characters, he brings about the big question: must we be good, haunted by an inherited guilt for being necessarily sinful humans, or can we be good, and follow our freedom to build our own morals and, at the end of the day, our conception of a worthy life? Lee brings that directly into his little sermons to the boys as they grow up and eventually take some weird turns, but more than that, he is such a precious character who pulls the plot away from the white-centered society we are dealing with. As an Asian American from San Francisco, we follow many of his struggles with xenophobia. In his grappling with belonging in a white elitist society or in his estrangement from his Chinese roots after being so far from home, his camouflage-like lifestyle is intriguingly heightened. And so, I have listed plenty of the show's historically relevant and poignant undertones, but I want to clarify that all of these big philosophical and cultural questions are, in the end, undertones. The show I watched, and I hope you will as well, is complex and nuanced, but it is also energetic and truly impactful. I was ecstatic about the great locations, the awesome acting, and the liveliness in the storytelling and the filming of everything in this series. There is a quote from the book that doesn't appear in the adaptation directly but that I think works beautifully to synthesize what these seven episodes are all about: "Now that you don't have to be perfect, you can be good." This show definitely embraced the flaws of its characters. Although it has some ups and downs, as every book adaptation does when choosing what to focus on, I think that, by choosing not to be the perfect book adaptation or the perfect historical depiction, it was able to be good. It was simply, but not simplistically, human.

articles.title: Canine minds: Brian Hare and experiments on the behavior of dogs
articles.description: During the COVID-19 pandemic, videos of the "What the Fluff" challenge circulated widely on social media. In these videos, owners would throw a blanket and step behind a curtain or wall, surprising their dogs when they suddenly vanished. Videos of dogs' seemingly surprised or startled reactions grew increasingly popular. Although these videos are fun and entertaining, the trend also gets at a more interesting question: what is really happening in a dog's mind? Brian Hare, a guest speaker hosted by the Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences on Nov. 11, investigates this question. Hare is a professor of Evolutionary Anthropology as well as Psychology and Neuroscience at Duke University where he conducts research focused on the social and cognitive abilities of dogs. Hare has authored several books on the dog mind alongside his wife and colleague Vanessa Woods, including The Genius of Dogs (2013) and Puppy Kindergarten (2024). To investigate dog cognition, Hare's lab developed a simple experiment in which dogs watched their owners hide behind one of two large screens. The screens were then moved, allowing the owner to secretly switch hiding places. Researchers subsequently revealed that the original hiding palace was empty and observed where the dogs searched for their owners. Initially, Hare tested whether the dogs could track unfamiliar experimenters, but the animals performed no better than chance. When the researchers repeated the experiment using the owners of the dogs rather than strangers, however, many of the dogs were able to successfully locate them. Hare suggested that this experiment may suggest dogs have secondary representation, which is the ability to think about things beyond what you are directly in the present. For example, it allows you to imagine where you may have left your keys, or think about what may happen tomorrow. Prior to this experiment, there was not a lot of evidence suggesting that dogs had this ability. Now, based on the results, the motivation and cognition linked with secondary representation seem to be tied to social connection with the owner. Hare describes this phenomenon as 'their motivation to remember.' Hare continued to investigate how flexibly dogs could solve problems, particularly those involving communication with humans. In another experiment, dogs were shown a wooden block placed next to a hidden reward. When a person placed the block while the dog was present, the dogs used the block's position to locate the reward. Interestingly, even after learning the block marked the reward's location, dogs stopped using its position as an indicator when they didn't see a person place the block. "When you take the human away, [the block] is meaningless, because it's no longer communicative," Hare said. Hare then compared the cognitive abilities of dogs, chimpanzees and infant humans. Across a series of eight social and physical puzzles, dogs performed more similarly to young children than chimpanzees did when solving problems involving cooperation and communication with humans. Chimpanzees, meanwhile, performed better than the dogs on tasks involving reasoning. So, where and how did dogs develop these social abilities? To investigate the evolutionary origins of dog cognitions, Hare's team compared dog puppies with wolf puppies that were intensively raised around humans. Over seven years, members of Hare's lab raised four dozen wolf puppies, constantly exposing them to humans even more extensively than experienced by the dogs in the study. Despite their early experiences, dog puppies were approximately 30 times more likely to approach strangers than the wolves. They also made more eye contact and were better at interpreting human gestures. When it came to non-social cognitive abilities such as memory and self-control, however, wolf puppies performed just as well as dogs. Importantly, wolf puppies that were raised closely with humans remained interested in the particular people who raised them, but their attraction did not generalize to strangers. Dog puppies, on the other hand, were curious and excited when meeting unfamiliar humans. Hare proposed that the ability of dogs to communicate cooperatively with humans may have developed through domestication, the same process that gives them floppy ears and curly tails. "When you have fear replaced by attraction, new forms of cooperation are born," Hare explained. To determine whether dogs' cognitive abilities can be identified early in life and predict their future performance, Hare's team partnered with Canine Companions to conduct a longitudinal study following puppies from approximately eight to 50 weeks old. Researchers assessed their cognition and temperament while comparing different socialization approaches. Surprisingly, all that extra socializing didn't make much difference in the puppies' cognitive abilities, suggesting you might not need to worry too much about your new puppy's social life. The researchers also found that several cognitive abilities associated with successful working-dog training emerged before 60 weeks. Perhaps you picture an ape capable of learning sign language or a dolphin with an impressive memory when you think of genius animals. Across all of these experiments, however, Hare's research suggests that dogs have their own unique kind of intelligence. As Hare puts it, "The genius of dogs… is their ability to understand, cooperate, and communicate with humans."

articles.title: What to do about measles? Dr. Aaron Milstone on the current situation
articles.description: As of Nov. 14, the United States has had its measles-free status officially revoked by the Pan-American Health Organization. This marks the loss of a 26-year long streak of holding said status. Measles is a highly contagious and airborne viral disease with no standard treatment. Symptoms can include high fever, rashes, and even death. The disease is best known for affecting children, although any age can be at risk. However, the response to measles has been one of the best-known success stories for vaccinations in terms of mitigating disease spread. Two doses of MMR vaccines administered during early childhood have long served as standard procedure by doctors to confer lifetime protection on the vaccinated against the disease. Measles is thus recognised as a fully preventable disease, with the vaccine demonstrating minimal side effects for the majority of the population. The recent increase in measles incidence and even fatality across the United States is therefore a concern for healthcare professionals. In an interview with The News-Letter, Dr. Aaron Milstone, a professor of Pediatrics at Hopkins specializing in infectious disease, provided his insights into the current situation. As a member of the American Academy of Pediatrics, Milstone stressed the changes in vaccination protocols experienced by the organization. "[The American Academy of Pediatrics] now provide the vaccine schedule that many states are pointing to since the CDC's CHIP schedule has… diverted from other recommended schedules over the last two years, so that's the first time in decades where our schedules have been different. And since it's changed, I think people are now referring to some of the professional societies for vaccine recommendations instead of the CDC." Milstone attributed some of the increase in vaccine hesitancy to the confusion introduced by the Trump administration into the necessary schedules and procedures for the vaccination process. "The reason we didn't have measles in the U.S. for decades was because of the success of the vaccine program," he said. "The reason that we are having sustained spread now is because that program has faltered. So this is completely due to decay in vaccine uptake in the United States." While the current circumstances may not be entirely the result of short-term vaccine denialism when considering that several school age children are the main victims of the uptick in measles cases, Milstone nonetheless highlighted resistance to vaccination as an increasing problem. This struggle is especially concerning as no viable treatments exist for those with measles, despite some investigations into the effects of nutrients like vitamin A. Though typical precautions including staying hydrated and other forms of supportive care can be carried out, modern medicine becomes more helpless when symptoms like inflammation in the brain arise. "I think we're unfortunately going to learn more from measles now because historically… we didn't have lots of young adults getting measles infections. They had it as kids because everyone got measles. So now we're kind of at a new time where we're going to be learning more about measles in the 21st century in a country like the United States, as opposed to in a low and middle income country where we still see measles spreading." With the changing situation comes a change in the concerns of the parents who want to protect their children from diseases. Despite all of the data establishing the effectiveness and safety of the vaccine, some parents face a different problem for children too young to receive the vaccination who may still be exposed to measles during circumstances like travel. To combat these and further issues raised by the resurgence of measles, Milstone predicts a long road ahead. "It's gonna be a marathon. It's gonna be the long process of trying to increase vaccine uptake among the population. And I think what's important to note is if you look in Maryland, the rates of the vaccine in kids entering kindergarten is still very high. Those numbers don't capture kids who are homeschooled or kids who are in communities that are [more isolated]... We have to figure out how we can target resources and effort towards communities that we know have a higher proportion of under vaccinated people because that's where the [biggest] risks are right now." Despite these immense tasks and difficulties to surmount, Milstone emphasized the need for advocacy and action at every level, especially from the student body. "Hopkins is filled with students that are young and idealistic and are interested in public health. A lot of people hear about measles and think, 'oh, this isn't there's nothing I can do because I've gotten my vaccine, I am protecting my community' but I think that what all people have to start remembering is that anyone can be an advocate for vaccine education… try to listen, actively listen, and have dialog with people in their community or in other communities that are concerned about vaccines with measles, and serve as everyday ambassadors... They don't all have to be people like me. You know, the people that spread misinformation are not scientists… We need an army of people to combat misinformation about vaccines and anti-science."

articles.title: A "crude" imitation
articles.description: Children, universally, will imitate adults. It's evident in the way they talk, the way they dress and the way they play. I can still remember how, at a party my parents attended (and dragged me along to), we kids would stumble across the floor and slur our speech until it became an incomprehensible babble - an effect of us deciding that the Capri Suns in the cooler were actually bottles of 80-proof vodka. Or, how after my naive second-grade self was assigned his own textbook for the very first time, believed himself to be just like a real-life college student - I carried that textbook under my arm with a sense of pride and maturity whenever I went to turn it in, blissfully unaware of how detached my fantasies were from reality. But the one thing that was off limits for us children to imitate was swear words. It seemed bizarre - what exactly was the reason to forbid this specific set of vocabulary? Surely, then, those exclamations must carry the weight of a thousand suns if they warranted those dreaded corner timeouts, the thousand lines we'd be forced to write swearing to never swear again - or for the unluckiest children, a bar of fresh soap for you to savor. (Dove always tasted better than Ivory.) Just like many things, however, the desire to grow up proved too strong, and we would parody those banned words. "Darn!" and "Dang it!" were common cries after a rogue kickball would inevitably bounce over the playground fence and into the street. Meanwhile, "Frick" and "Fudge" were reserved for the most serious offenses, such as being the first one eliminated from gaga ball. Yet these euphemisms never seemed good enough to me. They were too clunky; they gummed up one's throat, stopping you from wailing your most visceral emotions fluidly. I pondered this question for a day on the recess field. "Frick," I thought. "Frick, frick, frick." The "ric" sound snagged on my tongue. No good. I needed something smoother, something that could carry the full weight of my frustration. "Fuck." It was perfect. Now there was a word that could do it all - you could exclaim it in joy, or you could howl it in agony - and there would be no debate on the intensity of your emotion. Convinced that I had just revolutionized the English language, I wasted no time using it; judging by the wide-eyed looks on my first-grade classmates, I had clearly made a term so stunning that you couldn't not revere it. That lasted about five minutes before a classmate of mine pulled me to the side and told me that what I was saying was the actual F-word. Thinking back now, I definitely didn't make that word up myself. Although I grew up in a Chinese-speaking household, I must've heard that word somewhere before, possibly screamed by a hurried businessman sprinting to work or whispered by the old lady looking for her wallet in the checkout line, and I subsequently absorbed it into my vocabulary. It was something that I had picked up unconsciously, unaware that it had made its way into my life. That story always comes to mind whenever I think about my own identity. I say "y'all" all the time because my elementary school teachers would do so. I brush my teeth with one arm propped up against the sink because that's what I watched my dad do as a kid. And those are only the influences I'm aware of. Whose vowels are rolled into mine when I speak? Which one of my friends' gaits do I mimic when I walk? Did a passerby, in the fleeting moments that our paths crossed, imprint some habit onto me that I've adopted ever since? If all my actions, if all my movements are influenced by other people, then what aspect of me is truly my own? Am I just a crude imitation of the people who surround me, like an AI model trying to mimic a human? But, I argue, does it matter? After all, Van Gogh did not invent the colors he used to paint The Starry Night, nor was Für Elise played on an instrument invented by Beethoven. Yet we recognize these works as distinctly their own - not because the individual components of their works are original, but because of the way they are brought together. Our ability to merge our experiences into something distinctly our own is what defines our individuality. We will never be fully unique - Picasso's art will always bear traces of Cézanne, and Kendrick Lamar's songs will always echo Tupac - but that is not necessarily a bad thing. I find solace, even pride, in knowing that everything I do, everything I think, is shaped by the people I've met. I am a vessel for them - I carry pieces of them into places they'll never visit, into conversations they'll never have and into the lives of people they'll never meet. I am, in a way, a tribute to them for the world to see. Daniel Wu is a freshman from Houston, Texas majoring in Molecular and Cellular Biology.

articles.title: Ringing Black Holes Offer Precision Tests of Relativity
articles.description: Black holes remain some of the most mysterious and awe-inspiring celestial objects ever studied. This primarily comes from the fact that they literally can’t be observed unless they interact with something in its surrounding environment, most notably a star. Adding to their mystery, several types of black holes exist, including free-floating black holes that drift independently throughout space, stellar-mass and are produced from exploding stars, and supermassive black holes that exist at the center of galaxies like our own. But arguably one of the most mind-blowing mysteries about black holes is figuring out what happens when they collide, and even merge.

articles.title: Dirty ice around young star Beta Pictoris suggests frequent collisions and sheds light on the system's formation
articles.description: In a recent study of infrared light collected by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), a group of astronomers detected ice for the first time around the young star Beta Pictoris. Researchers had expected ice around Beta Pictoris, but previous searches had not directly detected it. The study, published in Science, found that the ice is mostly noncrystalline and mixed with carbon dioxide. The team says these new details provide clues about the early formation of the Beta Pictoris system and collisions that may still be occurring.

articles.title: Arizona-Taiwan partnership opens Tucson semiconductor hub
articles.description: Arizona-Taiwan partnership opens Tucson semiconductor hub nprevenas Mon, 16 Nov 2026 - 10:01 Today The University of Arizona, Pima County and Taiwan's National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, or NYCU, have opened the Talent and Innovation Hub in downtown Tucson, providing a dedicated base for training students and growing business and partnerships in the semiconductor industry. Housed in the historic Pima County Roy Place Building, the hub, or TIH, brings together the universities, industry and economic development partners to deepen connections between the technology sectors in Arizona and Taiwan. "The Talent and Innovation Hub builds on the University of Arizona's decades of leadership in optical sciences and semiconductor research, and it points toward what comes next," said University of Arizona President Suresh Garimella. "By partnering with NYCU, an institution woven into the fabric of the global semiconductor industry, we are preparing students with technical skills as well as the language and cross-cultural fluency necessary to lead anywhere in the world this industry takes them. This hub is a bridge between Tucson and Taiwan, and between the promise of Arizona's growing semiconductor economy and the talent it demands." Semiconductors power technologies central to modern life, industry and the global economy, and advances in artificial intelligence and other fields are driving demand even higher. Arizona has become a national center of semiconductor investment, and the hub is designed to help supply the talent that growth requires. Through the TIH, university and community college students will have access to hands-on training, academic programs and advisors, student exchanges and employers recruiting prospective talent. "At NYCU, we have seen how close collaboration among universities, industry and government can help develop the talent and expertise that drive a thriving semiconductor industry," NYCU President Chi-Hung Lin said prior to the event. "With the opening of the Talent and Innovation Hub in Tucson, we are bringing that experience to Arizona and creating new opportunities on both sides of the Pacific." Pima County owns the building, at 44 N. Stone Ave., which dates to 1928, and has supported a downtown U of A presence there since 2011. The county has made space available for hub operations under a new memorandum of understanding with the university. The arrangement also allows industry partners to conduct limited operations at Pima County Roy Place, bringing professionals into closer contact with students and university partners. "Pima County is proud to be part of this partnership creating a dynamic hub for workforce development in the heart of downtown Tucson," Dr. Matt Heinz, vice chair of the Pima County Board of Supervisors, told attendees. "The opportunity is to align university talent, industry demand and public sector support so that Pima County students and workers can connect directly to the jobs of today and the future." In July, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., or TSMC, expanded its commitment to $265 billion for advanced semiconductor manufacturing facilities in Arizona, the largest foreign direct investment in U.S. history. "TSMC is committed to Arizona, and this type of collaboration is one of the reasons we're here," TSMC Arizona President Rose Castanares said during remarks at the launch. "We are actively recruiting and hiring now. Our ultimate goal is to provide good-paying jobs to Arizona communities for many years to come." An engine for semiconductor research and education The hub draws on the two universities' complementary strengths to bring students and faculty together through semiconductor education, joint research and industry partnerships while fostering language skills and cross-cultural understanding. NYCU, based in Hsinchu – known as Taiwan's Silicon Valley – combines applied research and strong executive talent development for the industry, with close ties to global chipmakers. The U of A brings decades of leadership in optical sciences and semiconductor research, including the Center for Environmentally Benign Semiconductor Manufacturing, founded in 1996 as a National Science Foundation Engineering Research Center, and the Center for Integrated Access Networks, which advanced silicon photonics for high-speed data networks and optical communication. Today, the university is a partner in WISPER, an NSF center developing next-generation 6G wireless technology. Friday's ribbon-cutting at Pima County Roy Place marked a milestone in a relationship formalized in January. Lin and additional NYCU leaders began their visit on Thursday at the U of A campus, where they continued solidifying plans for the hub in cooperation with Pima Community College, Maricopa Community Colleges, Arizona Western College and Northern Arizona University. Inclusion of these academic partners will link hands-on technician training directly to degree pathways, scaling Arizona's semiconductor workforce and enhancing the existing opportunities the university offers to learners at all levels. To introduce U of A students to the TIH, the U of A Office of Research and Partnerships, College of Engineering and Center for Semiconductor Manufacturing hosted the Wildcat Horizons Semiconductor and Engineering Fair on Thursday. The event connected students with employers recruiting for internships and entry-level positions and highlighted academic training and cross-cultural exchanges available through the hub. Pathways offered by the universities allow students to earn a degree through a series of smaller credentials. Starting in January 2027, the U of A College of Humanities will offer Beginning Chinese for Professionals as part of hub programming. As offerings expand, students in Arizona and Taiwan will work on shared projects and capstone collaborations to strengthen technical skills, communication and cross-cultural understanding. The U of A and NYCU are also exploring future joint initiatives beyond semiconductors, including potential research collaborations in artificial intelligence, space technology and quantum computing. Connecting higher education to state industry growth The initiative also is expected to help connect research discoveries with potential applications, create opportunities for startups and attract microelectronics companies to Southern Arizona. "The opening of the Talent and Innovation Hub reflects the strong partnership between Arizona and Taiwan and our shared commitment to advancing semiconductors, research, innovation and workforce development," said Sandra Watson, president and CEO of the Arizona Commerce Authority, prior to the event. "The hub serves as an important asset to connect talent, industry and academia across both regions while supporting Arizona's semiconductor ecosystem. Congratulations to the U of A, NYCU, Pima County and all of the partners who helped make this facility possible." Aligning university research with municipal growth is intended to help Tucson workers, students and local businesses directly benefit from the investments in the region. The opening is an exciting milestone that strengthens the city's global semiconductor leadership, said Tucson Mayor Regina Romero. "By bringing these pieces together under one roof, we're preparing Tucsonans for high-quality careers, connecting our world-class educational institutions with emerging industries and showing global companies Southern Arizona's leadership in the technologies shaping our economic future," Romero said. Story Categories Campus Life Science & Technology Strategic Imperatives By Katy Smith, Office of Research and Partnerships News Article Type News Media Contact(s) Stephanie Doster

articles.title: AI Companies Develop Decision Models to Avoid Hallucinations
articles.description: On 15 September, a startup called TypeSafe AI released a new AI model called Jev. The company’s broad, disruptive claims about Jev that turned heads: The company claimed that Jev, which it calls a “System One model” is cheaper, faster, and can’t hallucinate. TypeSafe AI’s marketing is an obvious shot across the bow of other AI companies and their large language models (LLMs), which, despite their capabilities in math and coding, are infamous for their cost and tendency to “hallucinate” factually incorrect replies. And the startup has certainly attracted both attention and investment. The company recently raised $870 million in funding at a valuation of $7.5 billion. But the most impressive metric of Jev’s success is arguably the many imitators it’s already spawned. Cloudflare, Amazon, OpenAI, and Microsoft quickly released “decision models” that imitate Jev’s capabilities. Start-ups, academic researchers, and independent enthusiasts have released dozens more. “I have to give Jev credit,” says Matt Mastracci, an independent developer who has trained and released several decision models including Djev, which Cloudflare cited as an inspiration for its own decision models. “It really brought decision models to the forefront. In six or seven weeks, we’ve seen dozens of models come out.” Jev’s Latency and Compute Advantages Most AI researchers would call Jev a decision model or decider model. TypeSafe AI’s branding of Jev as a System One model refers to a theory of cognition popularized by psychologist Daniel Kahneman in his book Thinking, Fast and Slow. In the book, Kahneman draws a line between fast, instinctive thought (System One) and slower, deliberate thought (System Two). TypeSafe AI argues that modern LLMs offer the second, but are too slow to provide the first. The company claims that Jev can provide end-to-end response latency between 70 and 500 milliseconds. By comparison, LLMs typically require at least several seconds, to provide a response, and more complicated tasks (like coding software from scratch) can take several hours. Independent testing backs up TypeSafe AI’s claims. A pre-print co-authored by Ramayya Krishnan, a professor of information systems at Carnegie Mellon University, along with several colleagues, found that Jev delivered a median latency of 150 milliseconds across several benchmarks designed to gauge decision accuracy, including RewardBench and JudgeBench. OpenAI’s most capable model at the time, GPT-6 Astra, delivered a median latency of 1.89 seconds. A faster reply is often a cheaper reply, because it requires less compute time, and that’s reflected in TypeSafe AI’s pricing. The startup charges US $0.042 per million input tokens and output tokens are free. By contrast, for GPT-6 Astra, ChatGPT charges $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. Even GPT-6 Luna, a variant of GPT-6 designed for fast, inexpensive inference, costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens. Mastracci says that lower latency and costs open opportunities to tackle tasks LLMs currently can’t handle.“You can think of content moderation, such as moderating a fire hose of social media posts, or an extremely busy chat room.” Michelle Chen, a group product manager at Cloudflare (which has released its own decision models, including Clef and Claric), is also bullish on what decision models can accomplish. “You can probably offload 80 percent of your typical LLM tasks to a System One model that is going to be so much faster and so much cheaper.” TypeSafe AI has offered few details about how Jev achieves its speed, but Jev’s open-weights imitators provide more transparency. For example, take Cloudflare’s Clef, an open-weights decision model which is free to download on Hugging Face. “With an LLM, when you’re generating an output token, it looks at all the previous tokens, and predicts the next output token,” explains Chen. This occurs in sequence, token after token, until an end token is reached. “Our decision models don’t do that. They just do a single forward pass, to generate one read of all the inputs, and then generate one output. That’s why it’s a lot faster.” How Decision Models Generalize Tasks Decision models based on an LLM, such as Clef (which is based on Alibaba’s Qwen LLM), still contain the neurons and transformer-based model architecture of an LLM. They still input and output tokens. However, the portions of the model that turn these tokens into text have been changed to constrain the output. “Jev can only answer questions with a predefined, structured answer format,” says Zhongyu Wei, a professor at Fudan University who is also a co-author of a study that benchmarks decision models and introduces an open-weight alternative, SII-Decision. “We give it a question and options such as A, B and C, and it must choose from those options, returning probabilities alongside its choice.” In one sense, decision models are a return to classifiers, a type of model that, as the name implies, learn to sort data into classes. They’re used in a wide range of tasks, including spam filters and face detection. “These kinds of models are not new,” says Chen. “It’s almost like a rebranding.” But decision models offer a key upgrade over prior classifiers: generalization. Mastracci explains that classifiers were traditionally created through domain-specific training. Decision models, though, retain the general intelligence of an LLM, and that makes them applicable to many situations. “You can pick it up off the shelf, you point it at your problem, and it works,” says Mastracci. Cloudflare is putting this advantage into practice. Before decision models, teams looking to use a classifier model had to “get a lot of data, stand up a machine learning team, and fine-tune” a model for the task, Chen says. Decision models eliminate this requirement, so one decision model can be used in many domains. Examples include flagging spam pull requests in Cloudflare’s GitHub documentation repository, catching spam and phishing emails, spotting phishing domains, detecting prompt-injection attacks on LLMs, and reading emails about internet backbone outages to judge whether they’ll affect Cloudflare’s services. Do Decision Models Really Stop Hallucinations? In programming, “type-safe” languages are designed so that operations mixing incompatible kinds of data—adding a number to a string, say—are rejected before the program runs rather than producing a bad result later. Decision models are similar in that they prevent the model from generating an unexpected reply. TypeSafe AI’s name makes the connection between type-safe programming and decision models part of the company’s marketing, and it builds on that to make a startling claim: Jev will never hallucinate. This is, strictly speaking, true. LLMs hallucinate because they calculate probabilities for tokens repeatedly across a huge vocabulary of possibilities and output many tokens. This leaves room for less probable tokens to lead a response astray, or for the model to deliver tokens that are probable based on the model’s training, but not correct in the context of the reply. Decision models, by contrast, only calculate probabilities among the pre-determined possibilities, and the most probable is chosen. This eliminates hallucination. However, Carnegie Mellon’s Krishnan cautions that “eliminating hallucinations in the output does not eliminate errors in decision-making.” He and his co-authors tested Jev by asking it to determine if answers to questions were correct. Jev performed well when the judgment could be easily reached by reading the prompt, but performance dropped off when the judgment required math or involved a logic puzzle. Wei and his co-authors report similar results in their own research. They found the best decision models can slightly beat the accuracy of LLMs when asked questions about document understanding, and score close to LLMs when asked questions related to tool use (such as choosing the correct software tool to call to perform a user’s task). However, decision models fall behind when asked questions in domains that require topic expertise, including medicine, finance, and law. “I think reasoning is a key factor,” says Wei. Reasoning allows an LLM to work though its response before it provides a final answer to the user. However, Wei adds that reasoning alone doesn’t explain the domain gaps in all cases, as some LLMs performed well even without reasoning. Wei says the methods used to train decision models can also be a factor, and used decision-specific training for SII-Decision. Yet decision models and LLMs don’t have to be competitors. Krishnan and his colleagues also tested passing Jev’s low-confidence answers to GPT-6 for additional consideration. The combination of models slightly beat the accuracy of GPT-6 alone, and did so at 41 percent of the cost. Wei thinks this “hybrid architecture” will become common. “The decision model can call an LLM to give a more detailed explanation. And an LLM can call a decision model for a quick judgment. I think that’s very flexible.”
